name: Wanano
confidence_why: Stenzel's 2004 reference grammar places Wanano stress on the final syllable of the root and reports Waltz & Waltz 2000 as agreeing that the primary accent is predictably root-final, and the only wrinkle is that Waltz & Waltz 1967 called Guanano stress 'emic' while Stenzel provisionally labels the whole pitch system tonal, a difference of framing rather than of placement.
catalog_citation: Stenzel, Kristine Sue. 2004. A Reference Grammar of Wanano. PhD dissertation, University of Colorado at Boulder. xxiii+429 pp. (open copy: Biblioteca Digital Curt Nimuendaju, etnolinguistica.org/tese:stenzel-2004)
catalog_locator: ch. 2, sec. 2.3.3 'Stress assignment', 2.3.3.1 (pp. 73-75) and 2.3.3.2 'Foot parameters' (pp. 76-77); sec. 2.5.1 'Tone or pitch accent?' p. 83; sec. 2.5.2 p. 85; sec. 2.5.3 (closing restrictions) p. 92
catalog_quote: The placement of stress in Wanano falls, in the great majority of cases, on the final syllable of the root. [...] we can analyze Wanano syllables as organized into either bimoraic feet (the predominate pattern corresponding to root morphemes) or monomoraic feet (weak or deficient feet corresponding primarily to bound inflectional and derivational morphemes). Internally, feet are right-headed (prominence is marked +). Thus, we understand the predominant pattern of final (rightmost) syllable stress attested in Wanano roots. [...] At the level of the foot, then, we find that the relevant parameter establishes feet as right-headed. However, parameters are set for different domains, and at the level of the phonological word, the parameter for prominence is set to the left. The result is that in a fully composed phonological word, it is the leftmost foot which is prominent. Since the leftmost foot in the word is always the root, we find a confluence of morphological and phonological prominence. [...] Summarizing what we have seen in this section, we can say that surface-level stress in Wanano is ultimately assigned at the level of the phonological word, but is the cumulative product of parameters set at the levels of syllables and feet.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Kotiria (guan1269) is not in the catalog. The only stress/accent/prosody-titled bibliography item is Stenzel 2007 IJAL 73(3) 'Glottalization and Other Suprasegmental Features in Wanano' (doi:10.1086/521730). The abstract says roots are lexically marked for nasalization and tone but makes no placement statement. The open Portuguese precursor (Stenzel 2005 ABRALIN, held by the project) gives the same analysis: four contrastive root melodies BAB/BA/AB/A and an H tone ('acento') normally on the second mora of the bimoraic root. Best first-hand statement read: Stenzel 2004 dissertation sec. 2.3.3.2 pp. 76-77 (already held by the project) — stress falls on the final syllable of the (bimoraic, right-headed) root, which is the leftmost and prominent foot of the phonological word; H tone co-occurs with this stress; system provisionally described as tonal; updated). Acquisition priority for the 2007 full text: medium (would refine the tone-melody analysis; the placement statement is already covered by Stenzel 2004/2005; Stenzel 2013 UNL grammar remains the likely best printed statement, not obtainable here).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable and root-bound: roots (word-initial, mostly bimoraic CV.CV / CV.V) form a right-headed foot and the word gives prominence to its leftmost foot, so primary stress falls on the final (second) syllable/mora of the root, i.e. normally the second syllable of the word; suffixes are unstressed. Pitch is analysed separately as lexical tone (root melodies (<L>)H and (<L>)HL spreading rightward through the phonological word), with the first H tone falling in the root and co-occurring with stress (p. 92); Stenzel notes the system matches Hyman's pitch accent prototype but provisionally labels it tonal.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described as such; Stenzel reports Waltz's view that H tones of any 'secondary accents' within a phonological word are lowered, one H peak per phonological word (p. 83).
new_statements.exceptions: 'in the great majority of cases' — monosyllabic roots that lost an initial syllable (ko 'water', ~ta 'rock', c. 60 roots per Waltz 2002) surface lengthened CV: and carry the stress; devoiced (C)V̥ syllables are never stressed; tonal melody AB/H roots (H on first mora) exist per Stenzel 2005 fn. 6, implying some root-initial H.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (root + suffixes; in compounds the leftmost head root governs); stress and H tone coincide on the root; statement concerns word-level forms, not phrase-level.
new_statements.identity_note: Wanano = Guanano = Kotiria (self-designation), same language guan1269 / ISO gvc; Stenzel's data are from Kotiria communities on the upper Vaupés (Brazil/Colombia border), Waltz & Waltz's from Colombian villages (Villa Fátima, Santa Cruz). No dialect split relevant to the stress statement is reported.

new_statements.relation_note: Same work as the two existing_statements (the 2005 UMI issue is the 2004 Colorado dissertation; PuRe file is AUDIENCE-restricted and pure.mpg.de sits behind an anti-bot page, not reachable by automated download, so the etnolinguistica digital copy was re-read). Confirms root-final stress with first H tone; adds the tonal-vs-pitch accent discussion and the one-H-per-word lowering of secondary accents.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the final (second) mora/syllable of the bimoraic root, which is always the leftmost foot of the phonological word; feet are right-headed and the word is left-prominent, so stress = root-final syllable. Weight is moraic (no coda effect, no contrastive length). Stress co-occurs with the first H tone of the root's lexical tonal melody (p. 92: 'the first H tone will occur in the root morpheme, co-occurring with stress'); Stenzel provisionally calls the system tonal rather than pitch accent (p. 84: 'for now, I will refer to the Wanano system as tonal').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such by Stenzel; p. 83, reporting Waltz & Waltz 2000:455: 'A H tone associated with any secondary accents within a phonological word is automatically lowered, as there is only one allowable H tone per phonological word. [..] Primary accent, associated with H tone is predictably located (for the majority of words) on the final syllable of verbal, nominal and adjectival roots.'
new_statements.exceptions: 'in the great majority of cases' (p. 76) and 'for the majority of words' (Waltz & Waltz 2000 as quoted p. 83); syllables of the atypical shape with a glottal coda are 'never stressed' (p. 73); surface stress is 'ultimately assigned at the level of the phonological word' (p. 77).
new_statements.identity_note: Stenzel 2004 describes Wanano (Kotiria) as spoken in the Brazilian Vaupés (Caruru Cachoeira area); Waltz & Waltz 1967 describe the Colombian Vaupés villages Villa Fátima and Santa Cruz and say the phonetic differences between them are slight. Same language (gvc), Colombian vs Brazilian sides of the Vaupés.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Guanano has a single stress-pitch prominence system (stress and high pitch coincide; pitch is not a separate phoneme as in Tucano). Stress is treated as phonemic ('emic'), since a few minimal pairs exist and it is 'not phonologically predictable', but it is 'quite regular on the grammatical level': regular stress falls on the last syllable of the stem (root) in verbs, nouns and adjectives, and certain suffixes (-gá emphatic imperative, -hí person marker, -éra negative) are inherently stressed. The phonological word is a stress group of 1-8 syllables whose peak is marked by high pitch; initial stressed vowels are phonetically long.
new_statements.secondary_stress: sec. 7, p. 35: stress groups are of two kinds, 'an equal-stress group which has two stresses coinciding with a monotone pitch pattern, /túahá/ [túahá] 'I have strength'' and 'an unequal-stress group consisting of a primary and secondary stress in that order, /píriakà/ [píriakà] 'tooth''; sec. 5 p. 32 also describes 'multiple stress' on three-syllable words (first+last stressed = monotone; first two stressed, last unstressed, in /thúáha/ 'I stay').
new_statements.exceptions: A few minimal stress contrasts (/thúáha/ 'I stay' vs /thuáha/ 'I walk with a cane'); noun-verb stress contrasts said to be predictable from context (/báha/ 'I take out' vs /bahá/ 'a large variety of parrot'; /wáʔi/ 'I gave' vs /waʔí/ 'fish'); inherently stressed suffixes -gá, -hí, -éra; in two-vowel clusters stress may fall on either vowel (sec. 6.5, p. 34); the flap /r/ (and in Santa Cruz /g/) never begins a stress group.
new_statements.identity_note: Guanano (Wanano/Kotiria), Eastern Tucanoan, as spoken at Villa Fatima and Santa Cruz on the lower Vaupes river, Colombia (fieldwork 1964-1965; consultants Jose Dario, Vicente Moscera, Americo Valencia); minor Villa Fatima / Santa Cruz dialect differences noted (voicing of stops, st- cluster, /g/ not stress-group-initial in Santa Cruz).

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Stenzel 2004 statement (stress on the final syllable of the root, co-occurring with H tone; Stenzel p. 83 in fact cites Waltz & Waltz for this). Adds the authors' own framing: stress and tone form one 'acento-tono' system, stress is lexically 'phonemic' (not phonologically predictable, a few minimal pairs) yet grammatically regular (root-final), inherently stressed suffixes, multiple stresses per word, primary+secondary 'unequal' stress groups, and pre-stress vowel devoicing. The catalog record itself has an empty rule, so nothing is contradicted. Identity: Colombian Vaupés Guanano of Villa Fátima and Santa Cruz (data 1964-65, speakers José Darío, Vicente Mosq…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Guanano has a combined stress-tone ('acento-tono') suprasegmental system rather than separate stress and tone phonemes (p. 29); stress co-occurs with high tone and is 'phonemic' (intro p. 30: 'un sistema de acento fonémico') in the sense that it is not phonologically predictable and a few minimal pairs exist, but it is grammatically regular: stress (= high tone) falls on the final syllable of verb, noun and adjective roots, and certain suffixes (emphatic imperative -gá, person marker -hi, negative -éra) are always stressed; words may carry more than one stress ('acento múltiple', e.g. /túahá/). Stressed initial vowels are phonetically lengthened; vowels devoice in pre-stress syllables between voiceless consonants.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p.38: stress groups (1-8 syllables) come in two categories; an 'unequal' stress group consists of a primary and a secondary stress in that order, e.g. /píriaka/ 'diente'. Multiple stresses on a three-syllable word give a level (monotone) high pitch across the stressed span (/túahá/ 'tengo fuerza'; /thúáha/ 'me quedo').
new_statements.exceptions: Minimal stress contrasts /thúáha/ 'me quedo' vs /thuáha/ 'camino con una caña'; verb-vs-noun contrasts /báha/ 'yo saco' vs /bahá/ 'variedad de loros', /wá?i/ 'yo di' vs /wa?í/ 'pez' (said to be predictable from syntactic context); inherently stressed suffixes -gá, -hi, -éra; in two-vowel clusters stress may fall on either vowel, no stress variation inside three-vowel clusters (single morpheme).
new_statements.identity_note: Waltz & Waltz 1972 and Waltz 1976 describe Colombian Guanano of the lower Vaupés (Villa Fátima and Santa Cruz, c. 16 km from the Brazilian border; data 1964-65; minor phonetic differences between the two villages, Villa Fátima showing voiced stops attributed to Desano contact). Stenzel 2004 (existing statement) describes Brazilian Kotiria/Wanano communities (Ilha de Inambu, Caruru Cachoeira, Arara). Same language (guan1269); no dialectal difference in accent placement is reported.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as Stenzel 2004 and Waltz & Waltz 1972: regular accent on the final syllable of the root, marked/realised as high tone, with a small set of accent-bearing suffixes. Adds only pedagogical detail (orthographic convention, which suffixes take the accent, emphatic final accent). Catalog record has no rule text, so no conflict. Identity: Colombian Guanano of the lower Vaupés (Villa Fátima area), same variety as the 1972 phonology.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Practical-orthography statement: word accent (realised as high tone) regularly falls on the last syllable of the root, so root-final accent is left unmarked; the acute is written only to distinguish tonally different homographs (bára H-L vs bara level). Certain suffixes attract the accent: negative -éra-, negative imperative -é-, imperative -gá with ta- 'come' (elsewhere -gá only under emphasis), and an emphatic form in which the final vowel of present/imperative/exhortative verbs changes and takes an 'irregular' final accent (p. 90). Vowel devoicing occurs in the pre-accent syllable between voiceless consonants (p. vii).
new_statements.exceptions: Tonal minimal pair bára 'él nada' vs bara 'se pudre' (level); mono- vs disyllabic-root pairs macá 'pueblo' vs máca 'caño'; accented suffixes -éra-, -é-, -gá (with ta-), emphatic final-vowel accent (wahagé, tagá); noa 'bueno' with accent on the o loses the plural adjective suffix -a (p. 35).
new_statements.identity_note: Waltz & Waltz 1972 and Waltz 1976 describe Colombian Guanano of the lower Vaupés (Villa Fátima and Santa Cruz, c. 16 km from the Brazilian border; data 1964-65; minor phonetic differences between the two villages, Villa Fátima showing voiced stops attributed to Desano contact). Stenzel 2004 (existing statement) describes Brazilian Kotiria/Wanano communities (Ilha de Inambu, Caruru Cachoeira, Arara). Same language (guan1269); no dialectal difference in accent placement is reported.

tone_statements.quote: Além de nasalização morfêmica, Kotiria e algumas outras línguas TO apresentam um segundo elemento supra-segmental de tom11, com melodias compostas por tons B(aixo) e A(lto). Nas transcrições fonéticas das palavras em (1)-(2) acima, tom B é não-marcado e tom A é marcado com acento agudo na vogal. Tons baixos e altos se combinam em quatro melodias básicas lexicalmente associadas a morfemas de raiz, por ordem de frequência — BAB, BA, AB e AA. Em (3) vemos alguns exemplos de pares de palavras que contrastam por suas melodias tonais.
tone_statements.translation: Besides morphemic nasalization, Kotiria and some other East Tukanoan languages have a second suprasegmental element, tone, with melodies composed of L(ow) and H(igh) tones. In the phonetic transcriptions of the words in (1)-(2) above, L tone is unmarked and H tone is marked with an acute accent on the vowel. Low and high tones combine into four basic melodies lexically associated with root morphemes, in order of frequency — LHL, LH, HL and HH. In (3) we see some examples of word pairs that contrast by their tonal melodies.

tone_statements.summary: Two tones, low (B) and high (A), form four lexical root melodies LHL, LH, HL, HH (counted here as melodies); most suffixes are toneless and take spread tone; one melody per phonological word.

tone_statements.quote: Uma característica notável das línguas TO da sub-região do Uaupés é a gradual elisão de material fonológico na margem esquerda das raízes, normalmente os onsets das sílabas iniciais com tom baixo. Esse processo é muito pronunciado em Kotiria, onde ocorreu a ampla elisão de sílabas inteiras ... Em comparação, pronomes independentes sempre têm pelo menos um tom alto. No mais, e em outros tipos de construções com nomes justapostos, como vemos em (8b), cada palavra fonológica contém um tom alto e há pausas entre palavras. ... Em todos os exemplos, o tom alto é indicado com acento agudo (´) e tom baixo não é marcado; ... Ver Stenzel (2007), para uma análise detalhada dos suprasegmentos em Kotiria: nasalização, tom e glotalização.
tone_statements.translation: A notable characteristic of the ET languages of the Vaupés sub-region is the gradual elision of phonological material at the left edge of roots, normally the onsets of low-toned initial syllables. This process is very pronounced in Kotiria, where whole syllables were widely elided ... By comparison, independent pronouns always have at least one high tone. Otherwise, and in other constructions with juxtaposed nouns, as in (8b), each phonological word contains a high tone and there are pauses between words. ... In all examples high tone is marked with an acute accent and low tone is unmarked; ... See Stenzel (2007) for a detailed analysis of the suprasegmentals of Kotiria: nasalization, tone and glottalization.

tone_statements.summary: H vs L tone; every phonological word contains (at least) one H; low-toned root-initial syllables historically elided; full system per Stenzel 2007.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on placement among what could be read: Stenzel 2004/2005 (root-final syllable = second mora of the bimoraic root, the word's leftmost and prominent foot, co-occurring with the first H tone) is the only full description opened, and it reports Waltz & Waltz 2000:455 as agreeing (primary accent with H tone predictably on the final syllable of verbal, nominal and adjectival roots for the majority of words). The one wrinkle is typological: the 1967 Waltz & Waltz chapter (only p. 26 readable) calls Guanano stress 'an emic stress system', i.e. phonemic, whereas Stenzel provisionally classifies the system as tonal (two-way H/L with lexical melodies) while noting that its single accent peak per phonological word looks like pitch accent; these are different framings of the same H-tone-cum-accent, not different placements. Works 0 and 2 (Waltz & Waltz 1972; Waltz 1976) could not be opened, so nothing they say is checked. No disagreement on placement: Waltz & Waltz 1967 (this volume), its 1972 Spanish translation, Waltz 1976 and Stenzel 2004 all put regular/primary stress on the last syllable of the stem/root, with a small set of inherently stressed suffixes and a few lexical minimal pairs. The only difference is analytic type: the 1967 chapter describes one 'stress-pitch' prominence system (high pitch coincides with and defines stress; explicitly 'rather than separate stress and pitch phonemes as in Tucano'), whereas Stenzel 2004 analyses contrastive lexical tonal melod…

sources.citation: Stenzel, Kristine Sue. 2004. A Reference Grammar of Wanano. PhD dissertation, University of Colorado at Boulder.
sources.quote: The placement of stress in Wanano falls, in the great majority of cases, on the final syllable of the root. [...] we can analyze Wanano syllables as organized into either bimoraic feet (the predominate pattern corresponding to root morphemes) or monomoraic feet (weak or deficient feet corresponding primarily to bound inflectional and derivational morphemes). Internally, feet are right-headed [...]. Thus, we understand the predominant pattern of final (rightmost) syllable stress attested in Wanano roots. [...] at the level of the phonological word, the parameter for prominence is set to the left. The result is that in a fully composed phonological word, it is the leftmost foot which is prominent. Since the leftmost foot in the word is always the root, we find a confluence of morphological and phonological prominence.
sources.locator: ch. 2, sec. 2.3.3.2 'Foot parameters', p. 76 (p. 99); summary p. 77; cf. sec. 2.5.1 p. 83 and sec. 2.5.4 p. 92
sources.note: Sec. 2.3.3 'Stress assignment' (pp. 73-77): no weight by rhyme shape; roots bimoraic; feet right-headed, word-level prominence leftmost; 'The placement of stress in Wanano falls, in the great majority of cases, on the final syllable of the root' (p.76); leftmost foot = root is prominent, so stress = root-final syllable. sources.quote: The major features of Guanano phonemics are (1) three series of stops, including voiceless aspirated and unaspirated plus a series of voiced stops, (2) voiceless vowels occuring in both nuclear and offellde [sic, scanned] positions of the syllable, (3) a strong, influential nasalization and (4) an emic stress system.
sources.locator: p. 26, sec. 1 'Introduction', final paragraph (Rosetta Project scan of that page)
sources.note: Compatible with, but less specific than, the catalog: it records that the original SIL analysts treated stress as phonemic ('emic'), which is the feature later analysed (Waltz & Waltz 2000 as reported by Stenzel 2004:83; Stenzel 2004 sec. 2.5) as an H/L tone system whose primary accent is predictably root-final. No placement statement is in the two open pages, so the 'lexical (unpredictable)' reading is only the literal sense of 'emic stress' and is held with low confidence.
